How to lay tile with less waste, with a worked example

The tile you need is not the floor area divided by the tile area. It depends on where the grid starts, which way the tile runs, how the rows are offset, and whether a piece cut off at one wall can be used at another. Three choices decide most of it.

Open the free tile layout optimizer

The three choices

The starting line. A grid started against one wall leaves whatever is left over at the opposite wall. If that is 2 cm, you have a sliver that breaks when cut and is the first thing the eye finds. Sliding the whole grid changes every cut in the room at once, and the best position is rarely the corner.

The bond. A straight grid lines the joints up. A half or one-third brick offset hides a slightly bowed plank and looks better in a long room, but every second row starts and ends with a part tile.

Offcut reuse. The 36 cm left over from the end of one plank is often the 36 cm piece you need at the next wall. Reusing offcuts is a packing problem: which cut pieces come out of which whole tiles with straight saw cuts. It cannot be done well by eye on more than a handful of pieces.

A worked example

An invented room is 3.67 × 5.12 m with a 1.7 × 1.5 m corner taken out (an L-shape), 10 mm gaps at the walls, 3 mm grout, a 2 mm saw cut and no cut narrower than 50 mm. Three invented tile options, each with an invented box price:

TileBest layout, tilesBoxes with 5% spareCost10% rule, boxes / costCorner start, no reuse, tiles
Plank 20 × 120 cm, 6 per box, $626712$74413 / $80682
Subway-size 30 × 60 cm, 8 per box, $719012$85213 / $923102
Large format 60 × 60 cm, 4 per box, $684613$88413 / $88457

The floor to cover is about 16.1 m². For the plank, the best layout is a straight grid started about 20 cm from the left wall, and it needs 67 tiles against a lower bound of 66 from the area that must be covered: it is within one tile of the best that could exist. The 10 percent rule asked for 73, and a corner start with every cut piece taking its own tile needed 82, which is 15 boxes and $930. For the large tile the best layout is a one-third brick, and it needs 46 tiles, but with 5 percent spare and whole boxes the cost is the same as the rule of thumb. The honest reading is that the rule of thumb cost the same for the large tile and about 9 percent more tile for the plank (73 against 67), so it is a fair starting guess but not a number to order from.

Notice what the table does not say: it does not say the plank is the better floor. It only says which of these three costs least to buy for this room. Look, durability, slip rating and installation cost are yours to weigh.

How to check your own room

  1. Measure the room as its bounding rectangle and add each tub, island or corner as a cut-out.
  2. Enter the tile sizes, tiles per box and prices of the options you are choosing between.
  3. Set your grout joint, the narrowest cut you will accept, and whether the tile can be turned or its offcuts reused.
  4. Compare tiles in the layout, boxes, cost and the number of slivers; then print or download the cutting list.

It is a heuristic: it tries many starting lines, bonds and orderings and keeps the best, which is not a proof that nothing cheaper exists. The lower bound shows how close it is. Walls are never perfectly square, so keep your own spare.

Common questions

How do I find where to start tiling a room?

Dry-lay a row of tiles across the room from the centre, or measure the leftover at each wall for a few starting lines. Tilers want equal, reasonably wide cuts at opposite walls rather than whole tiles at one wall and a thin sliver at the other. The optimizer tries many starting lines in both directions and rejects any layout with a cut narrower than the limit you set.

Is a brick pattern wasteful?

It usually needs a few more tiles than a straight grid because alternate rows start and end with a part tile, but the cut pieces from one end of a row often fit the other end, so the difference can be small. In the worked example the straight grid was the cheapest for the plank and a brick bond was the cheapest for the large tile, which is why the optimizer compares them.

Is the 10 percent rule enough?

Sometimes it overbuys and sometimes it does not cover the awkward room. In the worked example it asked for 73 plank tiles when the best layout needs 67, and a corner start with no offcut reuse needed 82. Rooms with cut-outs, thin planks and offset patterns move the answer in either direction, so lay the actual room out.

Why would a smaller number of tiles not mean the best choice?

Tiles come in boxes, and a different tile size has a different box size and price. The optimizer ranks tile options by the cost of whole boxes after spare, and shows tiles in the layout beside the rule of thumb so you can see where the box rounding changes the answer.

Pricing the job rather than the material? The flooring bid calculator and the kitchen tile backsplash bid calculator build a bid, and the cut list optimizer does the same job for sheets and boards.

How many tiles does this room really need?

Enter the room, any cut-outs and one or more tile sizes. The optimizer searches where the grid starts, which way the tile runs and how the rows are offset, reuses offcuts, and shows the layout that needs the fewest tiles and boxes without thin slivers, with a to-scale drawing and a cutting list.

How it is calculated

Floor: the room rectangle, inset by the wall gap, minus your cut-outs. Lengths are held as whole numbers (hundredths of a millimetre) so every figure can be checked exactly.

Layout search: for each tile option, the tile may run either way, the rows are straight or offset by a half or a third of a tile, and the grid is started at many positions in both directions, including against a wall and centred. Every candidate is turned into whole tiles, cut pieces and awkward pieces where a cut-out bites a tile. The leaders are refined with small shifts.

Offcut reuse: the cut pieces are packed into tiles by a guillotine packer: straight saw cuts only, the saw width allowed for, best-fit placement, and many seeded random orderings. It is repeatable: the same input gives the same plan.

Choosing: layouts with a cut narrower than your limit are set aside whenever a clean layout exists; then the fewest tiles wins, then the fewest cuts, then the widest narrowest cut. If every layout has a sliver you are told, and the one with the fewest is shown.

Checking: a separate checker rebuilds the grid from the chosen layout and confirms that every part of the floor that is not a grout joint is covered exactly once, that no piece touches a cut-out or the walls' gap, that every cut sits inside one purchased tile without overlapping another piece, and that the tile count adds up. A lower bound from the area that must be covered shows how close the plan can be to the best possible.

Not modelled: diagonal and herringbone layouts, tile thickness, uneven or out-of-square walls, doorway thresholds, patterned tile matching, shade variation between boxes, curved cuts, and extra breakage for difficult material. A tile with a cut-out in it counts as one whole tile and is never used for offcuts. Prices are only what you type. Unverified on a real floor: tested on hand-computed rooms and on random rooms checked for coverage, overlap and cutting.

Common questions

How much extra tile should I buy?

The common rule is the floor area divided by the tile area plus 10 percent, and more for diagonal or brick layouts. That rule ignores the room: the real number depends on where the grid starts, how the rows are offset and whether offcuts from one wall can be used at another. The optimizer lays out the actual room, packs the cut pieces into tiles and reports the tiles the layout needs; you add your own spare for breakage and future repairs, which is a separate setting here.

Where should I start laying tile in a room?

Not always in the corner. Starting at a wall leaves one wall with whole tiles and the opposite wall with whatever is left over, which can be a thin sliver that is hard to cut and looks bad. Centring the grid puts equal cuts at both walls. The optimizer tries many starting lines in both directions, rejects layouts with a cut narrower than the limit you set, and picks the one that needs the fewest tiles.

Does brick or offset bond use more tile than a straight grid?

Often a little more, because every second row starts and ends with a part tile. Rectangular tiles and planks are usually laid in a half or one-third offset to avoid long joints lining up and to hide slight bow in the tile. The optimizer compares the bonds you allow, so you can see what the pattern costs in tiles for your room instead of guessing.

How does reusing offcuts save tile?

A piece cut off the end of a row at one wall is often exactly the piece you need at the other wall, or a smaller piece can come out of the leftover. The optimizer treats each cut piece as a rectangle to be cut from a whole tile with straight saw cuts and packs them together, allowing for the saw kerf. You can switch reuse off if your tile has a pattern, a directional finish or breaks too easily to be cut twice.

What is the narrowest cut piece I should allow?

Many installers avoid pieces narrower than about 50 mm (2 inches) or a third of the tile, because thin strips crack when cut and are noticeable along a wall. The limit is yours to set. If every layout leaves a narrower piece, the tool says so and shows the layout with the fewest of them rather than pretending a clean one exists.

How do I handle a tub, an island or an L-shaped room?

Enter the room as its bounding rectangle and add each obstruction as a rectangle: how far from the left wall, how far from the back wall, its width and depth. An L-shaped room is a rectangle with one corner taken out. Tiles that a cut-out takes a bite from are counted as using a whole tile, which is a conservative simplification, and tiles under a cut-out are not counted.

Is this plan guaranteed to be the minimum?

No. The search tries many starting positions, orientations and bonds and the packer tries many orderings, but it is a heuristic and not a proof. It reports a lower bound from the area that must be covered so you can see how close the plan is to the best that could exist. An independent checker re-verifies every plan before it is shown.

Is my room or price information uploaded?

No. Everything runs in your browser from the figures you type, nothing is sent to a server, and there are no accounts. Anonymous feature counts stay in local storage on your device and can be switched off.
